title: 5 Best Physician Scheduling Software Options Compared
description: Five physician scheduling options for call and block schedules: a managed service, spreadsheets, QGenda, Lightning Bolt and Amion, by who builds the schedule.
content:
Summary

  • Physician scheduling is a rules problem. One program administrator put it at 4-8 hours a month, and fairness and the ACGME rules are what make it hard.
  • Scheduling tools differ significantly: self-service platforms (like QGenda) require you to build and manage schedules, while managed services deliver finished schedules for you.
  • A well-built schedule has a major impact on resident morale, with one study showing it can boost perceived fairness from 43% to 95%.
  • For programs looking to hand off this administrative burden, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard delivers finished schedules built to your rules, with the ACGME requirements where they apply, without you learning new software.

If you've ever spent a Sunday afternoon rebuilding a call schedule because two residents swapped shifts and it cascaded into six other conflicts, you already know the problem this article is about.

Call and block rotation schedules are two of the hardest scheduling problems in medicine. Each one demands simultaneous rule logic (who can cover what, when, under which conditions), fair call distribution (distributing desirable and undesirable shifts equitably across months), and the ACGME rules (the common duty hour limits plus whatever the specialty adds). And they're almost always interdependent: a resident's block assignment determines their clinic availability, which determines their call eligibility.

One program administrator put it this way in a discussion about scheduling tools: "It takes at least 4-8 hours a month to make the schedule," and "the first draft isn't the biggest pain. It's swapping duties last minute and maintaining fairness over months." That burden typically lands on a chief resident who has a full clinical load, is new to the role every year, and is expected to somehow retain the institutional scheduling knowledge their predecessor carried out the door.

This article evaluates five physician scheduling software options. The focus is on their ability to handle call schedule generation and block rotation management, not general feature breadth. We'll score each against a focused rubric and give you a clear picture of what each tool actually does for the person running the schedule.

Please note that we are Scheduling Wizard, a service that builds physician schedules, and that we included ourselves in this comparison. Read our entry with that in mind. The ordering is by who builds the schedule: a service, then the spreadsheet, then software and the platforms you publish through. Measure by cost or mobile apps and the order changes too. Other tools are described as their own users and documentation describe them.

The Evaluation Rubric

Each option is judged on three things:

1. Self-Service vs. Managed. Self-service tools hand you a platform and expect you to learn it, configure it, and operate it. Managed services take your rules and deliver a finished schedule. The difference matters most when the "operator" is a chief resident who changes every year.

2. Compliance Handling. There's a meaningful gap between flagging a duty hour violation after the fact and generating a schedule that is built to the requirements. The first leaves the puzzle with you; the second takes it off your plate.

3. Multi-Schedule Dependency Handling. Block, clinic, call, and attending schedules are not independent. A tool that builds each separately still leaves you manually reconciling the conflicts between them. True dependency handling means all schedule types are resolved together.

The 5 Best Physician Scheduling Software Options

1. Scheduling Wizard

Overview: Scheduling Wizard is a YC-backed (W26) managed scheduling service built for residency and fellowship programs, provider groups and practices. It's a done-for-you service, not software you license and operate. Programs submit their rules, preferences and requests, and receive the finished block, clinic, call and attending schedules, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. There is no platform to learn, no seat licenses, and no chief resident triaging configuration errors at midnight.

Backed by Y Combinator (W26) and currently serving 20+ hospitals and practices and 30+ departments, Scheduling Wizard is built around one core insight: the hardest part of medical scheduling is the rules underneath it, not the interface.

What it does for call and block schedules:

  • The ACGME requirements built in. We do not leave the rules to a check at the end; the requirements you tell us apply, including subspecialty ones, go in while the schedule is built.
  • All schedules built together. Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules are built together, so cross-schedule dependencies are resolved before the schedule is ever delivered.
  • Built-in fair call distribution. Equitable shift distribution is counted, not eyeballed.
  • Institutional continuity. Because it's a managed service, scheduling knowledge doesn't walk out the door when the chief resident rotates. The rules live with us, not in someone's head.
  • Your platform is up to you. Upload our schedules into the platform you already use, use the live view we build, or both.

Self-Service vs. Managed Fully Managed
Compliance Handling Built in

Best For: departments, provider groups and training programs that want the build off their plate and the finished schedule back, without touching a scheduling platform.

What you get: the finished schedule as an Excel or Google Sheets file, or on a custom live view we build for the group. 2. Excel / Google Sheets

Overview: The spreadsheet is still one of the most common ways physician schedules get built, including many that end up in the platforms below. It ranks second on that basis. It takes any rule, any exception and any local arrangement, and it takes them the moment you think of them. Sheets adds live collaboration and a change history, which is why many groups have moved off desktop Excel.

What it cannot do is reason about what it holds. Block and call schedules depend on each other, and a spreadsheet does not know that moving one breaks the other. It also does not remember why the schedule looks the way it does once the person who built it moves on.

Where programs tend to get stuck. Not at generating a draft, which most platforms do, but at everything after: confirming the draft holds, fixing what does not, and absorbing the effects of each fix. If that pass is still yours, the license has moved the work rather than removed it.

3. QGenda

Overview: QGenda is a widely used enterprise scheduling platform in healthcare. It works as a central hub for scheduling across provider types, with analytics, automated shift notifications and coverage dashboards.

For Call & Block Schedules: QGenda can handle complex rule sets, and its centralized view is useful for large organizations managing multiple departments. It is a self-service platform, so your team does the setup and the build. As one practitioner noted, "Getting QG to actually do what you want isn't easy, and learning how it works is very complicated." When it flags a conflict, your team decides how to resolve it.

Criterion Score
Self-Service vs. Managed Self-Service
Compliance Handling Rules and alerts, run by your team
Multi-Schedule Dependency Handling Capable, configured by your team

Best For: Large hospital systems with dedicated administrative staff who can invest the time to configure and maintain the platform, and who need a unified scheduling view across a broad provider network.

4. Lightning Bolt (by PerfectServe)

Overview: Lightning Bolt is a self-service physician scheduling software that goes beyond a blank canvas. It generates schedule suggestions based on rules you define. For residency programs, it supports complex structures like the 4+1 scheduling model, which separates inpatient and outpatient blocks to improve continuity of care and resident well-being.

For Call & Block Schedules: Lightning Bolt automates the first draft, which is a meaningful improvement over pure manual scheduling. Its Custom Tally Targets feature helps users track ACGME guideline adherence. Your team still reviews the draft and resolves conflicts, and on a complex call schedule that review can take real time.

Criterion Score
Self-Service vs. Managed Self-Service (with automation assists)
Compliance Handling Rule-Based Tracking & Suggestions
Multi-Schedule Dependency Handling Configurable, but user-managed

Best For: Programs that want more automation than a spreadsheet but still want hands-on control over the editing process and have the bandwidth to manage a self-service platform.

5. Amion

Overview: Amion is widely used in academic medicine, and most residents know the name. It is primarily a platform for publishing a schedule rather than building one. It provides a clean, accessible interface for publishing and sharing call and daily schedules across a department.

For Call & Block Schedules: Amion publishes the schedule rather than generating it. Whatever schedule you put in is what your team sees, so fairness and the ACGME rules depend on how the schedule was built before it went in. That's not a criticism; it does that job well, which is why so many programs use it. But it should not be evaluated as physician scheduling software in the building sense. Many Scheduling Wizard clients use Amion as their publishing layer: we build the schedule, and the program puts the finished schedule into Amion for day-to-day viewing.

Criterion Score
Self-Service vs. Managed Manual Self-Service
Compliance Handling Not its job (publishing)
Multi-Schedule Dependency Handling Not its job (publishing)

Best For: Programs that need a simple way to publish and share schedules that have already been built, whether manually or through a service like Scheduling Wizard.

Fairness: What a Well-Built Schedule Changes

It's easy to frame better scheduling as a productivity win. But the evidence suggests the stakes are higher than that.

A study published in Neurosurgery found that rebuilding the call schedule to written rules reduced call variation by 70% and increased residents' perception of scheduling fairness from 43% to 95%. That's the difference between a program where residents feel equitably treated and one where morale slowly erodes over twelve months of perceived imbalance.

Fairness in scheduling is one of those things that's nearly impossible to track mentally. As one scheduler described it: "The swaps, tracking fairness, and just carrying it in your head all month… that's what really adds up." When fair call distribution is counted rather than estimated, residents can see the count.

Which Option Fits Your Program

If you're comparing physician scheduling software for call schedules and block rotations:

  • QGenda and Lightning Bolt are both legitimate tools, but they require an operator. Someone has to learn the platform, configure the rules, generate drafts, resolve conflicts, and re-run the process every scheduling cycle. When that person is a chief resident with a 60-hour clinical week, the operational math doesn't always work.
  • Amion is a publishing platform. It has a place in many programs' stack, for publishing rather than building.
  • Scheduling Wizard is the managed service on this list. Your program sends its rules and receives the finished schedule, built to them, with no software to learn and nothing lost when the chief resident rotates out.

For programs tired of treating schedule creation as a recurring crisis that falls on whoever drew the short straw, Scheduling Wizard does the work for you.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a managed scheduling service and self-service software like QGenda?

A managed service delivers a finished schedule for you, while self-service software requires you to learn the platform and build the schedule yourself. With a managed service like Scheduling Wizard, you provide your rules and requests, and our team builds the schedule to them, with the ACGME requirements among them where they apply. Self-service tools like QGenda provide a powerful platform, but your team is responsible for all configuration, data entry, conflict resolution, and schedule generation.

How do you handle the ACGME rules for my specific subspecialty?

You lead on this part. Tell us which requirements apply to your program, the Common Program Requirements and whatever your Review Committee adds, and we write them down with you next to your own rules before the first build. We do not assume we know your subspecialty's requirements better than you.

Do we need to replace our current scheduling platform like Amion or QGenda?

No. Amion, QGenda or whatever you use now is yours to keep; it is entirely up to you. We build the schedule either way and deliver it as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Many programs upload our schedules straight into their platform for daily viewing; others use the live view, or both.

What information does a program need to provide to get started with a managed scheduling service?

To get started, you typically need to provide your roster of physicians, a list of all required shifts and rotations, individual requests (like vacations), and your specific fairness and ACGME rules. The process begins with an onboarding call where we gather all your rules, from individual needs to subspecialty duty hour rules and fairness goals (e.g., equal distribution of weekend calls). We write these rules down with you and build to them.

How does a schedule built to written rules handle fairness better than eyeballing it?

A schedule built to written fairness rules distributes desirable and undesirable shifts (like nights, weekends, and holidays) across all physicians over a defined period. While a human scheduler tries to "eyeball" fairness, it's nearly impossible to track every variable across a large team for a full year. A team that does this full time keeps call and weekend counts as even as the rules allow, and hands the tallies back with the schedule.
